teaser.text: Amazon is a shop, a service network, an advertising business, and a landlord of computing power. A dollar enters through a product sale, a seller fee, an ad, a subscription, or cloud usage, then leaves through goods, warehouses, delivery, data centers, content, and people before the remainder becomes operating income.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Amazon?

paragraphs.text: Revenue growth is the central operating assumption. The base case uses 13.5% in FY2026, supported by first-half revenue and guidance for the September quarter. It then uses 13.0%, 12.0% and 11.0%, as AWS capacity begins billing after the stated six-to-24-month lag. The bear path falls to 12.5%, 9.0%, 7.0% and 6.0% if AI demand leaves capacity underused. The bull path uses 14.5%, 16.5%, 15.5% and 14.0%, supported by AWS growth of 36.7% in June 2026 and constrained capacity.

The bear case assumes Amazon builds faster than customers consume. AWS growth slows, infrastructure remains underused, retail profitability faces delivery and seller-fee pressure, and cash generation weakens. Investors then reduce the multiple from 18x to 12x. The path produces $273.24 in October 2027 and $198.20 in October 2029, with 25% probability. The risk is credible because AWS billing can lag investment by six to 24 months, but current growth and constrained capacity argue against making it central.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Amazon really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow, or FCF, subtracts property and equipment purchases from operating cash. Amazon spent $131,819 million on those purchases in 2025, leaving much less cash after investment. Its reported FCF was $11,194 million because it included proceeds from equipment sales and incentives.

blocks.heading: What do investors pay for Amazon today?

paragraphs.text: Cash tells a different story because Amazon is building capacity. During the twelve months ended June 30, 2026, operating cash flow was $161.4 billion, but equipment purchases drove free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion. Free cash flow is the cash left after buying long-lived assets such as servers, data centers and delivery facilities. Accounting spreads those costs through depreciation, while cash flow records the purchase immediately.

earnings.title: Amazon earnings: date, guidance and results
earnings.meta_description: Amazon's next results are expected October 29, 2026; watch AWS capacity, operating profit and spending.
earnings.opening: Amazon's next results are expected on October 29, 2026. Watch whether AWS capacity becomes profitable customer usage.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers how Amazon's business works, who its rivals are, how management operates, and what risks it faces.

blocks.heading: What has Amazon guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Guidance is management’s expected range for a future period, not a result already earned. Amazon’s July forecast puts September-quarter sales at **$197,000–$202,000 million**. It puts operating income—the profit left after running the businesses, before interest and taxes—at **$22,500–$26,500 million**. Investors will compare the eventual result with that range and with analysts’ separate forecasts.

The larger commitment is capital expenditure, or capex: cash spent on assets that serve the business for years. Amazon raised expected 2026 cash capex from about **$200 billion** to about **$220 billion**, partly because memory prices are rising. Forecasts call for DRAM prices to rise **125%** in 2026 and NAND flash prices to rise **234%**. The same budget may therefore buy less computing capacity.

blocks.heading: How has Amazon's revenue and profit changed over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached $200,606 million, against $167,702 million in Q2 2025. Operating income rose to $27,461 million, lifting operating margin to 13.7%. Prime Day’s move into June helped the comparison, but the operating improvement was still meaningful.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Amazon's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next results announcement is estimated for **October 29, 2026**, though Amazon had not confirmed that date. Investors should compare September-quarter sales and operating income with July’s guidance, then examine December-quarter guidance and any change to spending or financing plans. A higher budget is more encouraging when it buys capacity than when it merely pays higher prices.
The clearest operating evidence will come from AWS: its growth, its customers and the returns on the infrastructure now being built.
